utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Before we hear this witness -- you may sit, you may sit -- before we hear the witness, I propose that we very quickly deal with two housekeeping matters at this point. First of all, the motion filed by Counsel Susak about the testimony of General Blaskic. I understand he is suggesting that we should admit into evidence the transcript for one or two hearings where General Blaskic testified. This is what you meant. Now, I wonder whether the Prosecutor could set out his views. Sorry, Counsel Susak would like -- very briefly, because -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, the point of this motion is only to get the transcript from the 25th of February, I think, 1993, and it relates to only one segment, and, that is to say, a meeting between Blaskic and Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak and Nikola Krizanovic. That is the only piece of information that I'm interested in, in view of the new facts which indicate that there was yet another meeting where Nenad Santic is mentioned, Ivica Vidovic nicknamed Jevco, and the others, and all of this in the house of Jozo Livancic. I believe that this is also an important point, so as to ascertain the actual state of affairs, and on this basis, that meeting could be judged as compared to the previous one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Regarding Mr. Susak's motion, I think it is in the first place a matter of principle, and the Tribunal, regarding a similar motion, already took a negative decision, that is that the witness, whether the transcript of a particular witness could be admitted into evidence, could not be completely -- because the witness could not be completely interrogated by the parties. I think beyond this principle, the matter, beyond this principle, that is that we should always take the same decisions. I do believe that the truth needs to be established, and I wish that this transcript be joined to the documents on the Tribunal. But I do not think we can take a fragment of testimony, and it should be the testimony in its entirety which should be included in the record; that is, the whole of this testimony, all the counts to which the Tribunal might be addressing. However, this particular case that we are talking about is not finished yet. It may yet be completed within the foreseeable future, but it is not yet. Therefore, we think that all of the dispositions and all the exhibits to which the witness may be referring should be added. I am referring both to the examination-in-chief and to the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: When you say "the whole of the testimony," do you mean the entire testimony of General Blaskic, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I think it would be advisable that the context of the testimony be known, and it might be dangerous, or perhaps hazardous, or perhaps damaging, if only a fragment of this testimony were admitted by the Tribunal. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that this testimony as such, the transcript of the testimony given by General Blaskic on the 25th of February, cannot be admitted into evidence. Counsel Susak has a very easy way out, namely, simply to call General Blaskic to give evidence here in court after he has finished his testimony in the Blaskic case. Then he can be questioned about this specific issue and other issues relating to Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course I understand what you say, but I'm seriously concerned. Why is the Prosecutor evading the date of the 15th of April at 22.00 hours, when this meeting was held, and this was on the eve of the conflict on the 16th? That is what I wish to say in this context, and we are going to decide whether we are going to call Blaskic as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So therefore the motion is not granted, and the Trial Chamber has indicated how the Defence counsel for Josipovic could settle the matter by, as I say, calling General Blaskic. (Trial Chamber deliberates)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: In addition, as Judge Mumba has just suggested to us, it is of course open to Counsel Susak to call the other persons who attended that meeting. You could call them to give evidence in court in addition to Mr. Blaskic. All right. Now, to move quickly to the other question, I remember we left a question in abeyance, namely, when we should call the three Court witnesses that were mentioned a few days ago. I wonder whether Defence counsel have, possibly in consultation with the Prosecutor, come to some sort of agreement. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac, do you remember we discussed this issue of when we should call them?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecutor said that any date would suit him. Since we are talking about two of our witnesses, we think it would be advisable to call them at the very beginning, that is to say, when the trial recommences in May. As far as we are concerned, they can be called then, but then I have another proposal related to Toma Alilovic. That is the witness who was supposed to testify today. He did not come. The Defence believes that he is quite an important witness because he was in the house with Jozo Alilovic on the 16th of April, and the witness who testified in this Court said in his statement, in response to the Prosecutor, that he saw Tomo Alilovic in the house as well. In his testimony, this witness says that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic came on that day, and we believe that this testimony would be very important for us. However, the witness has not appeared, and we would like to suggest that this witness be called as a Court witness when the trial recommences in May. He is in Germany. If possible, we are going to submit this in writing, if you cannot rule this way. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. As for the court witnesses, yes, we do intend to summon them for the 3rd of May. Actually, the three of them. Not only the two you just suggested but also the third one. As for Mr. Tomo Alilovic, you didn't explain why he is not coming, and so we don't see why he should be turned into a court witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: We do not even know why he's not coming. We have been in touch with him, and we've been asking him to come for quite some time now, and I think in a way he's been rejecting to do so. On the other hand, I think that in order to ascertain the factual state of affairs it is indispensable to have his testimony. What I'm trying to say is that he is avoiding to appear before the court. We do not have any information as to his incapacity to appear, but we think that in order to ascertain the material truth, that is to say, what actually happened on that day, his statement is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, we do appreciate that his statement is important. On the other hand, we don't want -- this practice which we started here of calling court witnesses should be -- lead to abuses. The more so because, as you may remember, we started off thinking of court witnesses for those people who, since they belonged to a particular ethnic group, were rather reluctant to come over if called by Defence counsel. So for the sake of safeguarding the rights of the Defence, we thought we should take over and call them as court witnesses. But as I say, in this particular case we don't see why we should take action as such. We could ask you to make inquiries and try to approach the witness or a potential witness and try to understand why he's not coming. If he refuses and gives you convincing reasons, you could probably ask the court to subpoena this witness. Since he's in Germany, we could issue a subpoena. But as I say, we don't want to turn him into a court witness. Therefore, for the 3rd of May, for that week starting on the 3rd of May, and we have five working days, we could hear the three court witnesses plus, hopefully, Mr. Tomo Alilovic, plus one or two witnesses the Defence intend to call. Two more, yes. Yes, six or seven witnesses altogether. All right. We may now move on to our next witness. I think it is Mr. Fafulovic. Mr. Fafulovic, I'm sorry that you had to stay there while we were discussing procedural matters. Mr. Fafulovic, good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fafulovic. First of all, would you please introduce yourself to the Court. That is to say, give your name, surname, your father's name, the date of your birth, and your address.

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning. I am Fafulovic. I was born on the 20th of December, 1965 in Travnik. I live in Vitez, in a smaller village called Sofa, Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a house number?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 69. My father's name is Mustafa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many brothers and sisters do you have?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I have two brothers and a sister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, who did you live with? Who is your family?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: My family are my wife, my father, and daughter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, did you have a job? If you did, where?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: When? At the beginning of what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, did you have a job?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had a job. I worked in the work organisation Slobodan Princip Seljo in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Until the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first conflict or the second conflict?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: The last conflict, the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what are you by religion?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim by religion and a Romany by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you get to meet them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I met them while we were still working in this same work organisation where they worked too, but I got to know them better when I got involved in folk dancing in 1982.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, concerning this folklore, what position did they have?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Kupreskic, he was a choreographer, he taught us how to dance. Mirjan played the accordion, and they also danced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of this folklore group?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of this group of ours was mixed. There were Muslims, Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when? Until when was the composition mixed?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: It was a mixed composition almost until the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you remember a performance at the beginning of 1993 on Bajram?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a performance in Mahala, in the Muslim settlement, on the occasion of the holiday of Bajram. Do you remember what you danced?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: We danced dances from all over the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you dance dances that belonged to the Muslim or Bosniak people?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, at the end of 1992 and the beginning of '93, did you ever see Zoran or Mirjan Kupreskic in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see them carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when the war was over and when shares were being given out, did you get any shares?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You got these shares as what? Were you a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I was in an HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: We had uniforms belonging to the civilian defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any members of your family get killed during the war, injured?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My brother, he lost his leg. He's 100 per cent disabled. My father was wounded in both legs and in his right hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village that you said that you live in is predominantly populated by what population?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: It is mostly the Romany population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying it's not Muslims, Bosniaks, or Croats, they're exclusively Romany?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, more or less exclusively Romany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The folklore group that Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic belonged to, did it continue to operate after the war?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did, because I continued to dance as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they join a new society now?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now it is the Croatian cultural society, Napredak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how did this happen that you came to join this society? You're not a Croat, and how come you joined this cultural and arts society? At whose initiative did this happen, and could you describe all of this for us a bit?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: This was in 1994. Zoran sent me a message that I should come so that we could discuss something. When I came to rehearsal they had already started dancing, and I came and a colleague of mine, Delic Ahmed, who is not here, he also sent him a message to come, and when we came he asked whether we wanted to dance again, and we accepted this and we continued to dance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, Delic Ahmed, he's a Bosniak or a Romany?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Zoran tried to talk him to dance again as a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't talk him into it because he simply made him an offer because he danced before the war too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So he did not talk him into it, but he just made him an offer and this one accepted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us, do you remember when you last saw Zoran before the outbreak of the war, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but this was probably at rehearsal, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not recall the date?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not recall the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what did you do a day before the war began?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I was at work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I used to work in the morning anyway, and I came home at 3.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you find out that the war broke out on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was at home. I was getting ready to go to work. In the morning the shooting started, so I knew that the war began. I knew that something was wrong. I was taken by surprise. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were mobilised in the civil defence. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you were mobilised in the civil defence immediately, on the day the war broke out, or a bit later?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: We were included later. When the war broke out, we were there in the village. For four or five days no one touched us. After that, since no one came, we stayed there. The Croat side was closer to us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Oh, so that is how you opted for the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, how many days after the outbreak of the war were you included in the civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: It was around the 20th, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you find your village on this map?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try, if I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. If you cannot orient yourself, then you're simply going to say so and we're going to give up on this exercise. Would you please get up and take the pointer that is somewhere around there, pull it out, and try to find this and show it to us?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's somewhere around here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please stand to the side a bit and show this to the Court? Is that where your village was, where you lived?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Tell me, when the war stopped and when you all met once again, did you also have guest performances outside Bosnia-Herzegovina with this folklore group?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely why Zoran called us in, because there weren't enough members. He asked us to come, and he explained to us that night that we had to get ready, the entire group, I mean, because we were supposed to have several concerts in town and also elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was this elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Elsewhere was in Switzerland and Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I know you did as a group, but you personally, did you go? Did you personally go?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: No, I personally did not go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, very short notice was given, so we couldn't get all the documents we needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now, if you were to be asked about the attitude of Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic towards persons of a different ethnicity, what would you say? Were they persons who hated Muslims, who did not want to have anything to do with Muslims, or were they of a different orientation, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I think that they were always the same. They never made any difference between us as a group and others in terms of ethnicity. I think that telling proof of this is the fact that he called me and this other colleague of mine, Ahmed Delic, to continue dancing. As far as Mirjan is concerned, at rehearsals, during the break he would play Muslim, and Serb, and Croat dances, and then we would dance to that music in order to get going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perform during the war?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Serb and Muslim music was only used to get ready for the actual rehearsal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you very much. I have no further questions. I do not think there were too many questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume there are no other Defence counsel wanting to question the witness. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Several questions, not very many. Cross-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Fafulovic. My name is Franck Terrier, and I'm counsel for the Prosecution, and I should like to ask you some questions regarding your testimony. You told us that you were a member of the Romany community. Could you please tell us if this affiliation entailed any consequences in the municipality of Vitez that we are concerned with, that is, in '92, '93. I mean socially, or with regard to employment, or perhaps politically. I am not asking you with regard to the accused. I'm asking you about the life, about the public and political life in the municipality of Vitez at the time. Did your particular affiliation entail any consequences?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Not really, socially speaking. I was employed with that army company, Slobodan Princip Seljo, you know that, and the important thing was to have money so I have some means of livelihood. As for politics, we're not really much concerned with it. I mean, the Romany generally are not interested in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if, during the conflict which broke out between the Muslim and the Croat community towards the end of '92 and the beginning of 1993, did the Romany community take part or, rather, did it opt for one side or the other, or what did it do?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean? Was it neutral? I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you simply this: In the conflict which broke out in 1992 and 1993, did you and other members of your community take sides? Did you support one or the other?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We joined the Croatian army since we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Territorial Defence during the conflict with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Until the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When do you think -- could you tell us the date when, to your mind, the conflict began?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: With Muslims?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that that was what you meant by "the conflict." Do you know the date? You told us that you remained a member of the Territorial Defence until the beginning of the conflict, so could you please tell us, when did the conflict begin?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, until the conflict with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did your activities until the 16th of April involve?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your activities? What did you do on the 16th of April and the following days?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, as I told you, I was working, and I am a cook, a qualified cook, and I worked as a cook. On the 16th, I was at home already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened? Did something happen that day, in your view?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us in a few words, what was it that happened?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was in the morning, and I was getting ready to go to work, and suddenly I heard a whiz of shells, and bullets fired from rifles, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what else do you remember of that day, the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were then all at home, that is, in our locality. Nobody went out at all. We stayed in until Croatian soldiers came, and they requested that we stay there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we agreed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that mean that you sided with one side?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had to accept one side. The Muslims did not come first. These came the first, so we sided with them. We spent some five or six days at home, and we were there and nobody laid a finger on us, so we accepted or cooperated with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are not saying that you were forced to cooperate with the Croats. Does that mean that you were detained on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: No, we were simply there. The circumstances were such it was between the Croat and the Muslim side. That is important. Because of our safety, they came, and we accepted them because we are right between -- in between the Muslims and the -- between the Muslims and Croats. That is where the -- how shall I call it -- the demarcation line is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in the hours that followed this contact with the HVO, or the following days? I'm referring to you personally. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we agreed to everything. We were at home in the house, I and two brothers and father and my uncle and my aunt. We talked there, and we reached an agreement, and we accepted, like the majority of others who were in the village there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Fafulovic, I don't quite understand. What did you accept, you and the members of your family? Could you tell us what it is that you agreed to?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we agreed to come under the Croat army because they were the only ones who offered us protection and safety, so we agreed to be with them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, and in practical terms, what did it mean to be with them? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: You mean during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day and in the days that followed.

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that day, we were there, indoors, and the next day we moved a bit higher up. That is, we were not in our village. We pulled out to a higher place, to a hill, and that is where we practically spent almost the whole war. We were also accommodated in houses there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do there in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: We were mobilised, and I was a member of a labour platoon. Not only me, I mean, everybody else too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us, what is a labour platoon?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a labour platoon is -- it was made of several of us, not only Romany. There were also Croats who were digging trenches and cross-trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Fafulovic, can I then sum up your testimony correctly if I say that on the 16th of April, you were approached by the HVO forces who asked you to join them, you agreed to -- I don't know whether you agreed of your own free-will or not, at any rate, but you joined them and then you were sent to dig the trenches?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend is insinuating something to the witness which he did not say. He said that on the 16th, they contacted the witness. He did not say they were contacted by the HVO on the 16th of April, but later, five or six days later, said the witness. So will you please not lead the witness, but remember what he said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But the Prosecution asked a question. He asked the witness to say if that was so, whether this was what he said, whether it reflected the truth, and it is up to the witness to say "yes" or "no." I think that nobody was forcing the hand of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I was about to ask the question, yes. I shall rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which date, Mr. Fafulovic -- you must have already told us, but I'm asking you to repeat it -- on what date, exactly, were you contacted by the HVO forces which asked you to join them?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date, but it must have been five or six days after the conflict broke out, but we were mostly -- all of the time we spent in the village, and nobody came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fafulovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Only one question. Re-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke about fighting, that is about the 16th of April, could you please describe the fighting to us. Was it heavy fighting? Or if you did not see it, was it intense fire, or what? In one sentence.

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was early in the morning, more or less. First, one heard guns two or three times, and it was mostly bullets fired from rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the fire come only from one side or was there shooting from various sides?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I could not really tell because I was indoors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a question for the witness. Mr. Fafulovic, you said that you saw, on many occasions, Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. My question is as follows. On what occasions would you usually meet Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic? What sort of occasions? Simply when you went to the folklore group? Or other occasions, say, at work, or in the street, or -- could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was mostly at work, and folklore, when we danced. Then we socialised in coffee pubs and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see them or talk with them in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Therefore, where do you normally meet them? You said at work or a folklore group, and where was it? In what particular locality?

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: It was mostly in the company where I worked because I was a cook there. So during lunchtime, when I would distribute lunch, they would come to have lunch, and folklore, when we danced, in the cinema hall in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Thank you so much for testifying, and you may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADIL FAFULOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand we are going to hear Mr. Veljko Kato (sic)? Yes? Cato. Cato. Because now you didn't put the accent. I mean, this is your fault. I remember you insisted so much when the Prosecutor produced these documents, and now we never find these wonderful accents so we can understand whether you say "Kato" or "Cato." (The witness entered court) Anyway, good morning, Mr. Cato. Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Lordship.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Cato. Are you comfortable, and are your earphones all right? Will you please tell us your name?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: My name is Veljko Cato. I was born on the 24th of July, 1960, in Vitez. I'm a Serb by ethnic origin. I was born in Vitez, and I've lived in Vitez all my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your address? Where do you reside?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Hrvatske Mladosti 45.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what did you do in 1992? That is, rather, where did you work, and what were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: In 1992, I worked as a head salesman in the furniture store in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when did you work there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: I worked there until August '92.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do after that, and why did you stop working there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: After that, I asked for my -- I went on a holiday, but I had to report to the company so they could keep a record.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, actually, you were laid off?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you laid off? What happened to that store of yours?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Because in the warehouse of my company, they now placed humanitarian relief and medicines that were brought, so all the storage space we had was used for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So those were medicines, donated medicines?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These medical supplies, they were used for all ethnic groups and all structures in Vitez; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as this humanitarian relief was stored in your store. Were you then included in some organisation?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes. I was included in the civil defence, the Territorial Defence, because I had the keys to the store.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Territorial Defence pay your salary?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that who paid you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: After that my company continued paying out my salary because I was still their employee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us specifically when you received your salary from the Territorial Defence? Was it when it finally fell -- that is, when the Croats left the Territorial Defence in October or November?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: No, no. It was earlier than that. I believe it was September. I do not remember exactly, but I do think it was September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That job which had to do with the control of those medicines, that is something that you did until the beginning of the war; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then when the war began?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: When the war began, well, then I was not working for my company any more.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel speak up? We cannot hear her.

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: When the war began I was with the first aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: I was a driver. I drove a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were incorporated in the medical service; is that so?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Until -- I don't remember exactly but it must have been July of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Then I was incorporated in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were on the front line?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a soldier?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can say what you like. I do not really have to ask you everything, so you can say whatever you like. Tell us, since you were of Serb ethnic origin, did you have any problems in this regard after the elections, say, that is, since late 1990 until the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: No, I did not have any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any problems concerning the Serb ethnicity in the territory of the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: No, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in Tolovici, in the village of Tolovici?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: In the village of Tolovici? I don't recall exactly whether -- I don't remember if there was a conflict, but the Serbs left Tolovici in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who they clashed with, I mean, Serbs from Tolovici?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Serbs from Tolovici had a conflict with Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That village was completely evacuated. The Serbs fled and left the village?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other areas around Vitez that you know have been abandoned by Serbs under the Muslim pressure?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: No, there were no other areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were you doing on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, '93, I went to report to my company and then, together with Zdravko Vrebac, I dropped by the store where Mirjan Kupreskic worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is that shop?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: That shop is in the building belonging to Vucjak, in the southern part of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you get there and how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: We got there around 12.00 and stayed there until about 3.00, except that Zdravko Vrebac purchased things for his shop straightaway and went back immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Zdravko Vrebac have?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: At that time, Zdravko Vrebac had a coffee bar called Set.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you find in that store?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: In that store we found Ivo Grabovac, Gavro Mujcibabic, and Batric Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then? Did you talk? Did you sit down?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Then we moved to a part -- to the storage space there, and we had a couple of drinks and talked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk politics, political tension, political problems in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: No, we did not discuss politics or the political situation in Vitez. We simply told jokes and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that day, did you see Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: No. No, I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mirjan Kupreskic go on working after the cease-fire of 1994?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Mirjan Kupreskic began to work some 10 days or 15 days after the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As what? Do you know where he worked?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Same job which he held before, that is, in the Vucjak building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he worked there without interruption, that is, throughout '94, '95, '96?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes, he did work there without interruption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Zoran Kupreskic worked, and when did he resume working there? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Zoran Kupreskic went on working -- resumed, continued working immediately after the conflict, perhaps a month or so later, and he worked up there at Vitezit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you meet Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic? How long have you known them?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Zoran Kupreskic, I met in 1978, when the cultural folklore society, Slobodan Princip Seljo, was founded. Mirjan Kupreskic, I met in 1982 when he came back from school and joined the cultural folklore society Slobodan Princip Seljo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did Mirjan Kupreskic attend school?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Mirjan Kupreskic attended school in Trstenik, in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the chairman of that cultural folklore society, SPS?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Their last -- the President of the cultural society was Senad Besic, and the last chairman of the society was Zaid Hidic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These two persons, Senad Besic and Zaid Hidic, are they Muslims or Croats?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: They're Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the name of the society changed? Why was it done and when were other societies set up in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: After the elections, the cultural society, Slobodan Princip Seljo, was renamed the City Cultural Folklore Company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there some other companies after the -- were they set up after the elections?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: After the elections in Vitez, we had Preporod, the Muslim cultural folklore company, and the Croat one called Napredak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the difference between them?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Well, the difference was that the Napredak Croat cultural company included members of the Croat people. Preporod brought together members of the Muslim people, and the town cultural company of Vitez remained mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, these were mono-ethnic companies exclusively, that is, the Croat one, that is, the Muslim one?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, how did the people in this cultural society of yours socialise? You came there for rehearsals, and did you see them apart from these rehearsals?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes. We would see each other after the rehearsals. We would socialise. We went to each other's homes when our children had birthdays and on all other occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you celebrate your national holidays together?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend weddings? Were there any mixed marriages within the society?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were mixed marriages within the society. Nevzudin Ahmic married Vesna Pavlovic. Zoran Kupreskic married a girl who danced in our society too. There were marriages there among the dancers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you call on one another over the holidays?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall where you were for Bajram in 1993, and with whom?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Bajram 1993? Zoran Kupreskic, with his wife Mira Kupreskic; Mirjan, with his wife Ljubica; and I with my wife Lenka. We all went to Mustafa Dzidic's for Bajram in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mustafa Dzidic is a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did you go to each other's homes?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend each other's weddings, and were you best men at each other's weddings, and godfather's to children and things like that?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes. When Ljubica, Mirjan Kupreskic's wife, was supposed to have her first baby, Mirjan Kupreskic told me that if he would get a son that I would be his godfather, and that if he had a daughter, that my mother -- daughter would be the godmother. Since the first baby was a girl then my wife was the baby's godmother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you think about this offer? What did it seem like to you?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: I was pleased by the offer because godparents are supposed to be friends, good friends, but there was something strange about it because I am a member of the Orthodox Church and I was supposed to be godparent in a Catholic church, and that was a kind gesture by Mirjan Kupreskic. When he said, "We'll take care of all of that. The important thing is that we are good friends."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, you've known Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic for about 20 years. Can you tell us what kind of people they are?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes, I've known them for about 20 years. They're very honest, family men, people who are always ready to help others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they interested in? What were they involved in?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: They were mostly interested in folklore, in dancing, and in socialising. Mirjan Kupreskic also played in restaurants and at weddings. That is to say, they were only interested in music, dance, and socialising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what their attitude was towards the members of other nationalities, other ethnic groups? The way that Mirjan Kupreskic behaved to you, is that the way the two of them behaved towards the Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Their attitude was the same towards Muslims and all others. Mirjan Kupreskic's best man was also a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the persons who they were close to from the Muslim community?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: They were close with Fahran Ahmic, who played the drums in our society, and all the others who danced there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us one more thing. Until the war, you were involved in folklore. How often did you have rehearsals, how many times a week?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Twice a week we had rehearsals, and if we were supposed to go out for a guest performance then we would have more rehearsals than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perform and rehearse all the way up to the outbreak of the conflict, the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when Zoran and Mirjan started playing and dancing at the folklore group again after the war?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: We got together immediately after the cease-fire, after the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who got together there, this cultural society?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Again, we had the core of the old dancers there with us, Croats, Serbs, Muslims, Romany, and all of those who wanted to continue working.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume there now is cross-examination by the Defence counsel. Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Cross-examined by Mr. Blaxill:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Cato. My name is Michael Blaxill. I'm one of the Prosecution attorneys assigned to this case, and I have just, literally, a handful of questions to ask you, if I may. On the 15th of April, 1993, did you see Mr. Zoran Kupreskic at all?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: In 1993, I did not see Zoran Kupreskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, you said that you did see Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic, and you left Mirjan's place of work at about 3.00 in the afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: On that day I saw Mirjan Kupreskic, and we were together about two to three hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you said that you left there about 3.00 in the afternoon, and Mirjan Kupreskic stayed on at his place of work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: I left the shop around 3.00, and Mirjan Kupreskic stayed at his place of work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day, the 16th of April, 1993, can you tell us where you were, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: On the 16th, I was at my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see either Mr. Zoran or Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic during that day, the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see either of them on the following day, the 17th of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, 1993, I didn't see either Mirjan or Zoran.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when was the next time you did, in fact, see Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: The next time I saw Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic was about a month or a month and a half later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that for a period of time you worked in first aid, in driving for medical aid; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me who organised your work, or who commanded the sort of unit you worked for of medical-aid drivers?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Medical-aid drivers had their work organised by the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the person within that Territorial Defence who had that responsibility? Do you know the name?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: I do not recall the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe from about July 1993 you were then engaged in fighting on the front line; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain as a soldier at the front lines?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: I was not a soldier at the front line. I was there at home. I was on the line at my home until the cease-fire in February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your period of being thus deployed at your home in the defence of your home territory, do you recall seeing Mr. Zoran or Mr. Mirjan Kupreskic at all?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: I remember seeing them then because I went to see them when their father died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any form of regular contact with them during that period, or was that just the one occasion?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: That was the one occasion when I went. We did not have any contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm obliged. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Cato, tell us why people did not go to Ahmici often during the war and why people from Pirici and Santici didn't go to Vitez very often. What was the situation like there?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: The situation was such that one could not pass that way. There were war operations going on, there were snipers, and the road was not passable. So when one went, one had to go on foot, taking another road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall where the actual front line was in Ahmici -- or rather in Pirici and Santici? Was it close to the village?

utterances.speaker: VELJKO CATO
utterances.text: I do not recall, but I think it was close to the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We don't have any questions for the witness. Mr. Cato, thank you for testifying. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Let us call the next witness, Marko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may interpose for a moment, I do have an observation in relation to this next witness. The Prosecution have not been provided with any form of summary relating to the potential evidence of the witness, and as I recall the general terms of agreement some time ago, when my learned friend, Mr. Terrier, was dealing with the Defence directly about this issue, essentially we said that we would not insist on such statements or summaries primarily for character witnesses. I am just wondering whether, therefore, my learned friends would be in a position to confirm that, as there has been no summary delivered, is the evidence of Mr. Marko Martinovic to be restricted purely to issues of character, and indeed within that context? We have heard the word "character" used in a different context, as to propensity for conduct, but I mean genuine character witness. Perhaps that could be clarified because, obviously, I would have an objection to proceeding without summary if that is not so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we told Mr. Terrier earlier on that this was a character witness only. We hadn't even talked to this witness earlier ourselves. We simply brought him in to say what he thought about these men because he knew them well. So our colleague, Mr. Terrier, agreed on that occasion with this, so he did not insist on a summary. But we have another problem because our next witness will be coming in at 10.30, so please, could we have the break now and then have him testify after that because he will be coming in at 10.30, and then we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you speak of the next witness, are you thinking of Marko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: He is not around? He is not here?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: He is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We will take the usual 30-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Martinovic. Could you please stand and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic, we have all woken up, so we can begin, can we?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: We can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself to the Court first, that is to say, your name, surname, your father's name, your date of birth, and your address?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Marko Martinovic. I'm a writer. I was born on the 8th of March, 1933. My father's name is Ivo. I was born in Travnik, and I now live in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were a writer. Are you a member of a writer's association or something?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm a member of two associations. I'm a member of the Writer's Association of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the other one?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: The other one is of Herceg-Bosna, the Association of Writers of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, as a writer, what kind of literature have you been writing?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I've mostly been writing short stories. I've written poetry too. I've also written essays. I was also involved in journalism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these features, reports, and journalism, do you consider that to be journalism for newspapers only or for the electronic media as well?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I mostly worked for newspapers, and I also worked for a local TV station and made reports for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These reports and these newspapers that you worked for, were you also active in 1992, and before the war, in 1993, and after the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I also worked in the post office, and I also worked as a journalist. I wrote about culture, and I recorded interesting people in villages and interesting crafts and arts that were dying out. I also made some amusing shows, entertainment, where we all talked to each other nicely, Muslims, Croats, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So tell me, in your reports and in your literary work, did you advocate any political views or did you write neutrally in terms of politics?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I never advocated any political views, naturally, except if something was more in the interest of the Croat people. I do not have such stories, reports, or any writings that would fan hatred. After the war, I got a golden prize in Zagreb for a book of short stories that was published, and also the reviews published were very flattering, and they emphasised my goodness, my humanism. I also heard Muslims say that they liked the book. Although I talked a bit about the war, I talked about the cease-fire more, and attempts made to have a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To have a reconciliation?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to have a reconciliation too. The name of the book is "Jesus in the Basement."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a pretentious title, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I spent a lot of time in the basement too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Zoran and Mirjan Kupreskic. I've known them for a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I met them as people who were involved in cultural activities. They were involved in the cultural society of Slobodan Princip Seljo. They played and danced there. Then in '91, after the elections -- I don't know what year this was -- it was chained into the society of -- the town society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this cultural and art society, Slobodan Princip Seljo, was this a mono-ethnic society or a multi-ethnic society?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Princip Seljo was a multi-ethnic society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they sang and danced, was it only songs and dances of one ethnic group, or all the nations and nationalities of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: They played and danced everything from Macedonia to Slovenia, and they also wore national costumes from Slavonia, from Sumarija, Serbia, and also --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever wear a fez?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's this Bosniak costume with a fez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the elections in 1991, did you join political developments in Vitez in any way? I'm not asking about culture. I'm asking you about politics.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I was never involved in politics but, as I said, until the present day, I have not been a member of any political party, but I'm one of the founders of the Croatian cultural society called Napredak. As soon as it was founded in 1991 or, rather, it existed even before that but it was banned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did it exist, until when?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? I'll try to give some brief information about this. In 1902, this cultural society was founded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in the days of Austro-Hungary?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, there were four cultural societies, one of the Jews, one of the Muslims, one of the Croats, and one of the Serbs, and that's the way it was until 1948 when all of these societies were abolished, that is to say, all of those that belonged to an ethnic group. Naturally, after the elections, these societies were renewed, that is to say, these ethnic societies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who are the people who renewed in Napredak in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I know. I did, and Franjo Kurevija, Fra Bozo Blazevic, Zdravko Pavlovic. There were quite a few of us. We had an initiative committee, and I thought that in that way one could strive for one's interests and one culture and not by weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that you were one of the co-founders of this renewed cultural society of Napredak?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As one of the refounders, you weren't really a founder because it was first founded in 1902. Did you have any contacts with Mirjan and Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I did, on several occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With Zoran or with Mirjan?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: With both, one and the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I tried to get them to come to Napredak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Because they were true masters, and we needed choreographers, and musicians, and dancers. As the cultural and art society of Napredak, we did not have people of this kind. Although, that is not the only point, to have folklore, but we're also supposed to publish books and to study history, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're talking about this cultural and art society, and you've been using an abbreviation; haven't you?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I've been using this abbreviation for cultural and art society, but they didn't want to join us, you see, and I was sorry. On several occasions I had a heated discussion. I can't remember. Once we had a performance at the cinema and Napredak organised it, and we asked them to dance, and they didn't want to dance under the name of Napredak. This was already in 1992. Then I intervened, and the others wouldn't let them at all, and I intervened and -- I intervened so they could perform under the name of the Town Society. They danced at the time with Muslims, and Serbs, and others, and all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did they explain why they didn't want to go to Napredak, why, or did this question remain pending?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they did not like this division into national groups because they lived and worked together for some ten-odd years and they didn't like it this way. They didn't want to have a mono-ethnic society and become part of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether they also socialised with members of other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course they did. Until 1993, we all socialised together because I liked also to be with those artists. We would sit and have a drink or two and so. Until, one might say, the first day of war, everybody socialised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember one day before the war -- and we shall take at the beginning the war. The war began on the 16th. So I'm referring to the eve of it, that is the 15th of April. What were you doing then?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I could tell you every minute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I'm not asking you about every minute. What were you doing then?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I was out in a village. I was making a story about blacksmiths. Then I went home, had luncheon that afternoon. I went to the coffee bar Set and there I sought musicians who were with them. I saw Mirjan there. It was around 4.00 or 5.00. It is a coffee bar which does not accommodate more than four or five people. You can just sit at the bar and that's it. So we mostly, who had something to do with various arts, that is, we met there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, were there any Muslims there in that company?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Fahrudin Ahmic. I think he's a drummer. I saw him on the -- in the afternoon of the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about their activities after the war in that cultural society, now that you're in Napredak, because there are no other such companies; are there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, there are no other companies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if they also reactivated, animated, other people to join the society after the war?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: After the war, they joined Napredak because there was no other such societies. That was the aftermath of the war. But they were very active in their society, and they contributed a great deal to the study of our folklore. There were -- I think there still are some Muslims in our folklore company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any Serbs there?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there any Romany?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there are Romany too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about what they did when they heard they had been indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: My impression was the following: After the war, I saw them much more often than before the war. When we heard about the indictment and, again, we naturally were in a cafeteria, because where else? Everything begins and ends in a coffee bar, and you know what? I've been taking very many notes during the war because these were things that interested me, and a book I'm writing about the war perhaps will explain certain things. Perhaps it will explain them to me too. But as regards these two, well, naturally -- I don't know. They were flabbergasted. I asked them -- I was trying -- I put out some tentacles to learn more from them about these things, but I could not learn anything from them, nor can I do it now. As I look at them, I simply could not believe that they are indeed what the indictment purports them to be. I really don't see how they could do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of notes were you taking about Ahmici, for what?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's for my writing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you want to write something about --

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I want to write something about those characters, about those people, or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't get any useful information from them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No information. I didn't even have the impression that they played any important role or that they knew anything. That is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they perhaps think that they should establish contact with somebody in The Hague Tribunal to clarify their position?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I would not know. I do not know all the things that they did. What I do know is that they could not believe they had been accused. I don't really know what steps they took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you know if a letter was written, a letter to The Hague, about them?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that they wrote a letter through a journalist, Zvonko Cilic?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I think they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Wrote a letter of protest, but I don't remember that letter. It was a long time ago, three years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't remember the contents of the letter?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember --

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I read papers every day and ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that first conflict that took place?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: The first conflict, and the second one too completely astounded me. I was in the post office then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you yourself did not notice anything?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, will you tell us, in your literary language, how would you describe Zoran and Mirjan?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's much easier for me to put it on paper than speak because I'm not a good speaker, but I would describe them as good people, very dear to me, very broad-minded, interested in arts in general. With Zoran, I had an experience. When I heard that he had been accused, he borrowed from me books on oriental philosophy, Maharishi, Si Baba, and he wrote a lot about that. I think only a good man can do that. Yes, of course, he is a Catholic, but he also likes the writings of somebody -- or Si Baba or Maharishi. Mirjan, I know him as a married fellow, as a gay fellow. We often played billiards together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know them. Could you even imagine that they are people who could kill people?

utterances.speaker: MARKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I tried to say when they learned of the indictment. So naturally, we were all flabbergasted because I simply cannot believe that such people could do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: No cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No cross-examination. No questions. Thank you, Mr. Martinovic. I assume it you don't want to re-examine because there's been no cross-examination. Mr. Martinovic, thank you so much for giving evidence in court. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
